segments.title: THE PULL AT THE BENCH
segments.angle: How would I explain this idea if I had to tell it like a children's fairy tale?

sources.text: The Influence Of Others: “You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with”.
The Influence Of Others: You're the average of those around you, don't associate with average people.
The Influence Of Others: Who you allow to influence you will determine where you'll end up.
The Influence Of Others: Cut out all who drag you down or hinder your growth.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You've had that moment, right? Someone in a kitchen says you're the company you keep, and you nodded like it was the weather. When's the last time you actually counted the people you spend your days with? Did you count them? Or did you just feel them?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Gather close, March. Every good tale begins with a hearth and a hush. Once, in a village where the bakers all lived under one long roof, a girl was handed a sack of flour and told the old saying.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Which saying, exactly?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You are only the sum of the five who sit nearest you at the table. So every night she counted them, and every morning she woke a little more like whoever had been loudest the evening before.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So it's a counting problem. If your five are fine, you're fine. I can check that. Give me the sack...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: ...Patience. The tale does not say sum. It says average. An average is not a count. It's what comes out when the good and the poor sit at one table and meet in the middle. And the girl had been sitting near the middle all her life.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the middle's where you end up. So you pick people above it. Is that it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is it, March. Keep company with those who see the wide world, and their wide world becomes your ordinary. Keep company with the ordinary, and greatness turns into a fairy story for other people. The sack holds one more instruction. I shall keep it in my pocket until the flour is measured.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Withholding. Fine.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Plain version. Who you let in decides where you land. And the lie is that it's a sum. You're saying it's a pull.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely. The sum is a clerk's notion. The pull is a tide, and it does not ask permission before it moves the boats.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then I'll try it on me. Out loud. My five. The ones I spend the most time with. You, the timer, the notebook, whoever's listening to this, and J. Five. That's the list.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Brave, March.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Look at the sack, March. The stitching at the top has run into the shape of a crown. Every ordinary thing in a kitchen is a sign to a man with eyes. And I have eyes. Unlike you.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a bad stitch. Somebody's thread ran out.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, the timer. On an ordinary Tuesday it's the one I'm with longest, and it only ever asks me to go faster. That's the honest count.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So the timer drags you down, the notebook lifts you, and the crown sits over the whole kitchen. You are the sack's lesson, March, not the flour's. Move over, too. A chair that hears this much destiny ought to belong to a storyteller.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No chair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And write the names down before you decide what they mean. The clock's a clock. I'm not cutting out the clock. It's fine. The test is whether a voice only ever makes the bread worse. If one does, that's the one your note means by drags you down.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Cut out? Ah, the pocket opens at last. The old tale ends with scissors. The girl cut the ribbon on the sack that had spilled, and the loaves came out lighter for it, and the whole long house admired her in whispers.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Your scissors are a fairy tale. Gently. What did the guild actually do?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Scissors are truth, March.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The guild would not let an apprentice sell a single loaf until a senior baker vouched for him. He could knead like the wind and still stand at the back of the market with no stall at all, watching the crowd walk past him to someone else's counter.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A vouch is just another person's opinion. Average, possibly. Who said the senior baker was above the middle?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The senior baker was above the middle, March, by the width of a whole stall. That is the point. Every apprentice was told that whoever vouched for him would decide what he was allowed to bake. The guild had the sense to write that down.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, the tangent earned its keep. The guild knew who vouches for you shapes what you bake. That's a vouch, not a sum. You're right about that much.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For someone who believes this, March, the kitchen looks different. Each person at the bench is a small weight on the scale. The scale doesn't care how kind they are, only which way they push. Every morning you ask whether the people beside you are lifting the loaf or flattening it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the picture I'd keep. A question you ask at the bench before the dough goes in. Nothing more.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Late Edition, so here's one true thing. Then I'm back to the timer. I think J picks people who make him argue better. And I don't think he notices he does it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall drop the act for a line, March. I have never met him, and I think you are right.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Noted. Go on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I would write that down in gold, but the ink is cold and the hour is late.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the crust, March. That crack I heard earlier, like a sea-wall in its first storm. Tell me that was not an omen.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. You're right. Now the timer. Up next, It's Never Too Late To Change, then Habits Become Automatic, Your New Identity. I'm setting the timer, and you're not touching it.

segments.title: THE ONE PUSH-UP AND THE YEARS BEFORE IT
notes: It's Never Too Late To Change
Habits Become Automatic - Your New Identity
segments.angle: What is the opposite of this idea, and how could that also be valid?

sources.text: It's Never Too Late To Change: No matter how old you are, it's never too late to make a change in your life.
Habits Become Automatic - Your New Identity: Habits are a blessing and a curse. What you do repeatedly becomes automatic.

Habits Become Automatic - Your New Identity: Master the habit of showing up. If you show up at the gym five days in a row - even if it’s just for one push-up - you are casting votes for your new identity.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You've said 'that's just who I am' out loud. Maybe to a friend over a drink, maybe to yourself in the car.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then you watched them decide not to argue.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It felt like being let off. It also felt like being shelved.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Let me argue the other side, because somebody has to and you clearly won't. By a certain age your habits set like concrete...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: ...concrete. Ah, March. A fine word for a man who has stopped looking down.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Whatever you've done over and over becomes the floor you stand on. Change is a lovely idea for people who haven't finished setting yet. The rest of us are just getting more of the same.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note speaks plainly, so I shall read it to you at full size: 'No matter how old you are, it's never too late to make a change in your life.'

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every door in that sentence stands open. The best of the note I keep back until the kettle sings.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So you're saying old isn't a wall. It's a number.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And change is a verb, and a number doesn't get a vote.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Correct, March, though you have made it sound like a clerk's ledger.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Age is a number. Change is what a person does with their feet. The number sits in the corner while the feet walk out the door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let us walk it through on one push-up. A man has skipped the gym for a long stretch and has no plan to go back.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then one day he gets down on the floor and does one push-up. The next day, another. The streak reaches five days in a row, and the kettle clicks off on the word five.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Tell me, March. Is that a new man on the floor, or a man who did a push-up?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A man who did a push-up.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The kettle clicked because it's a kettle, and kettles click. Don't dress up the steam. It's just steam.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Steam is steam, I grant you.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note does not say he's a new man yet. It says every time he shows up he's casting a vote.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A vote needs no majority to count. It only needs casting, and the count is what he becomes, one ballot at a time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Votes are lovely until you look at the count.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Touché, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The count's been running for years. The note itself says what you do repeatedly becomes automatic. One push-up on a Tuesday doesn't switch off the other thing. The old routine is still on autopilot.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes, March, and that is the hard part. The automatic keeps running...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: ...The question is whether the one who starts can become the automatic. You are arguing my case in reverse, which is the honest way to argue it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, then how long before a change counts as a change?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A week? A year? At what point is it allowed to count at all?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the question you were circling, March, so I'll give you the hardest answer I have. A change counts from the morning it's made.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But the years before that dawn are not returned. Not one of them comes back to the bench, however many times the man gets down on the floor. He is older, and that is the price. I will not soften it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's bleak.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Thanks for that. Fine, then the opposite's real. Some things really are too late. Nobody gets to start again at the age they were when the door shut. You'd be daft to pretend otherwise.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Quite so. The opposite is right about the years...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: ...and wrong about what comes after. It is valid for what's gone and false for what's left. That is the whole trick, and the note only mentions half of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, test it on me. I keep a column.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every argument I win goes in it, and I don't decide to add a point. It just goes in. I'm not saying the total. But that's automatic, isn't it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So if I started a new column, it would be automatic too.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: There it is, March. The habit note says what you repeat becomes automatic. This note says it's never too late.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Cross them and the automatic that traps you turns out to be the same machine that can lock in something new. Change is repetition, not one brave decision.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One note gives you the trap, the other gives you the door, and the door is the same shape as the trap.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the thing that traps you is also the thing that lets you out.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Same wiring, opposite direction.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Same wiring. The wiring has never once cared which way it pulls.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the scary bit, though.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: If it doesn't care which way it pulls, then skipping the next morning is a vote for the old column. The note makes it sound like a gift. I'd call it a loaded door.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It is a loaded door, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes, I said so.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And that is exactly why the first push-up matters more than it looks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He isn't waiting for one heroic decision. Each morning is another ballot, and the casting makes the man.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For someone who believes this, a late change is a new automatic. You wake, the floor is cold, you do your one thing before the coffee, and you don't remember deciding.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The person who keeps casting that vote is slowly becoming the one who does it without thinking. That is the whole picture.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A cold floor, one thing before the coffee, no speech.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That I can use. Nothing about it needs a grand title.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then tell me the kettle is not a sign, March.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It clicks off just as I say Tuesday, and I would be a fool to call it chance.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The kettle clicked because it's a kettle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: But fine, I'll give you the omen, the one point I never meant to hand over. The rest of my column stays private.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the column is yours, March, and the kettle is mine.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But the years, which I will not soften, belong to nobody but the man who spent them.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Timer's going.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the close. Up next, the rest of It's Never Too Late To Change and the identity note. I'm the one who set the timer, so I'm the one who gets to hear it.

segments.title: THE FLYWHEEL AND THE CHART ON THE WALL
notes: It's Never Too Late To Change
Habits Become Automatic - Your New Identity
segments.angle: How was this problem (or a similar one) addressed in the past (e.g., 10, 50, 100 years ago)? What can be learned from previous attempts or contexts?

sources.text: It's Never Too Late To Change: No matter how old you are, it's never too late to make a change in your life.
Habits Become Automatic: What you do repeatedly becomes automatic.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're at the counter, kettle still rumbling, and the old story starts up again. Too set now. Too late for the new thing. Too far along to start over.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Most people think a change only counts when it's big and loud. Past a certain age the door's shut, and everyone nods like that's the sensible view.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Sensible. March, that view has the comfort of a sofa, and the sag of one too. Let me read the note as it stands. 'No matter how old you are, it's never too late to make a change in your life.'

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every word of that stands open like a gate. The best of it I keep back a while longer, so do not hurry me.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the door isn't shut. It's unlocked, for anyone willing to lean on it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Lean, yes. Though you have turned my gate into a lock, March. Let me read you what a lecturer said, long before our kettle was invented.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He called habit a great flywheel. The heavy thing that keeps the whole machine of society turning once it's up to speed. Once it spins, nobody has to push.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A flywheel. Lovely. But his listeners weren't told what to do on a Tuesday morning. He's describing the machine. Nobody's handing out spanners.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You've found the detail that carries the whole argument, March. A flywheel turns what it's given. The lecture gives the turning and leaves the hand to you.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. The flywheel's old and the hand's new. But I'm not convinced a lecture knows what my knees do on a cold floor.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It does not know your knees. It knows the turning, and your knees are where the turning meets the ground. Put the man from the cold floor under it. One push-up is a spoke, and the spinning turns the spoke around.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A spoke, a wheel, now a tyre. You're running out of vehicles, Narrator.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I shall pretend that was not a joke. A thing that turns can turn either way. That is the piece the other note was too shy to say.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sure you will.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: What you repeat becomes automatic. So the thing that's dragged me to the sofa is the same thing that could get me off it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Look at what the old lecture did, March. It warned about the spinning, and in the same breath it said the spinning can be turned on purpose. It held both halves at once.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hang on. You're turning a dead lecturer into a poster.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I would never put him on a poster. The poster is yours. I only read the spinning back to you, and the reading is my vanity, not his.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sure, sure.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, I'll give you that one. The Victorians pinned charts to the wall. A grid, a box for every morning you got up when you said you would, and a gold star when the box was ticked. Kids had them. Grown men had them too.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A chart pinned to the wall! March, that is the first notebook, a notebook that learned to stand up and be looked at. Shift over, too. I need a chair with a view of that wall.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a grid of boxes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Not a notebook. You can't fit a sentence in a box the size of a stamp.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then what do you keep, March? Some tally that never gets spoken aloud?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: ...Okay. I keep a column. Every point I win goes in it. I didn't decide to add it. It just goes in. Don't put that in your notebook.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then you have been keeping the Victorian chart in your head all along, March, and refusing it a grid.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's private. Nobody gets the total. You included.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Noted. A private column is still a record, and a record is a habit with a number on it. That is where the notes meet. I was hoping you would walk straight into it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The habit note says the repeated thing becomes automatic. The never-too-late note says the door stays open. The chart is where both are true at once, a ledger that makes the repeated thing visible so you can turn it. Neither note says that alone.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the chart's not a tyrant. It's the thing that shows you which way the spinning's going.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes. The old ones saw both halves together, the spinning and the choosing of which way to spin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A bit grand, but yeah. The habit note says you're stuck. The other says you're allowed out. Put them in one room and you get the chart.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For a person who takes this on board, a late change is a ledger they keep without noticing. Each small entry lands in the book of who they have become. Picture a bus station waiting room, a stranger with a pen, writing one line in a notebook nobody else will see.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: One line. No speech. Nobody reads it but them. That's the bit I like.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And each line lands in the book whether the writer feels grand or not.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. A waiting room and a biro. That's all it takes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the kettle, March. It clicked off on its own, and I have decided that is a sign.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A sign. Of what, exactly?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I offer J a title for it: Keeper of the Morning Votes. He cannot claim it yet, but I am patient, and patience is a virtue of the old.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'd hate that title, and he'd keep it on the wall anyway. You can have the title. I'm keeping the column.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And here's the comeback I saved. You want the chart, the kettle and my chair. You don't get the column. You don't get the total either.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the total stays yours, March, and the kettle goes to me. Who was right is left open, the way the gate is left open.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Left open... good. That's the honest answer. Next up, The Value of Time and Failure Is How We Learn And Grow. That's our time, so I'm the one saying it.
